note: Reel 14: The Jam With No Cause. A Bengaluru jam with nothing at its front; Sugiyama et al. 2008 (22 cars, a 230 m circle, one rule: drive steadily) made one from nothing; a small slowdown amplifies car by car until someone stops; the jam travels backwards at about bicycle speed (15 +/- 5 km/h on highways); the root cause is our late reactions; Stern et al. 2018: one controlled car on a 260 m ring dampened the waves (up to 40% less fuel); leave a gap: you could end a jam, or start it (the loop). Kokoro af_heart, speed 1.0. Numbers as words. 'Bengaluru' (Kannada [beŋɡəɭuːɾu]): misaki's plain spelling reads /bˈɛŋɡələɹˌu/, 'BENG-guh-luh-roo', the long 'loo' lost; the phoneme ear heard the third syllable as ɚ/ᵻ/ɪ in s01, s01b, s01c. s01d–g add an Indian e, a long uː and a tapped ɾ (all in Kokoro's vocabulary; there is no retroflex ɭ). Facts: docs/research.md.

lines.text: Follow it to the front: no accident, no signal, not even a pothole.
In two thousand eight, scientists in Japan made a jam out of nothing.
Twenty-two cars, one circle, one rule: keep a steady speed.
Then one driver slowed down. Just a little.
The one behind reacted a beat late and braked harder. The next, harder still, until someone stopped.
And the jam moved backwards, about as fast as a bicycle.
The driver who started it never knew.
That's the root cause: not the road. It's us, braking a beat too late.
In two thousand eighteen, one self-driving car on a ring like this held a steady speed.
So leave a gap. You could be the one who ends a jam.
Or the one who starts it.
